title: Understanding pedagogical challenges faced by technology teachers in special needs classrooms
abstract: <jats:p>Teaching learners with special educational needs requires dynamic and adaptive pedagogical strategies that can lead to social development and academic success. This can be possible if teachers are assisted in mitigating the daily challenges of teaching such learners. This qualitative exploratory case study investigated the pedagogical challenges encountered by two Grade 9 Technology teachers in the Capricorn District of Limpopo Province. This study used Shulman’s Content and Pedagogical Knowledge framework to understand teachers’ challenges. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews and classroom observations; all collected data were analysed thematically. This study found that teachers experienced various challenges, including the emotional labour of teaching, burnout in the LSEN environment and the enactment of instructional knowledge. The study concluded that the sampled teachers displayed weaknesses in lesson planning, activating learners’ prior knowledge, diagnosing errors, achieving curriculum objectives and sustaining engagement. As a result, it was recommended that support through teacher assistants, creative differentiated strategies and enhanced digital-technology literacy to improve outcomes for learners with special needs was imminent.</jats:p>

title: Integration of Biomechanics and Digital Technology: Using Kinovea for Motion Analysis and Learning for Beginner Athletes
abstract:
<jats:p>Background: The integration of biomechanics with digital motion-analysis technologies has introduced new approaches for examining movement efficiency, kinematic characteristics, and technical patterns in walking and running activities. Kinovea, as an accessible motion-analysis software, provides both visual and quantitative feedback. However, its application in supporting technique development among beginner athletes remains insufficiently explored.
Aim: This study aims to describe the use of Kinovea in biomechanics training and examine its contribution to the awareness of kinematic characteristics and movement techniques among beginner athletes.
Methods: A descriptive qualitative design involved 72 beginner athletes aged 18–25 years selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected over 16 weeks through interviews, field observations, and motion video recordings analyzed using Kinovea. Kinematic data focused on joint angles, stride behavior, and movement phases during walking, running, and the flight phase. Qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis with NVivo 12, while kinematic results were interpreted descriptively to identify performance patterns and areas for technical refinement.
Result: Kinematic analysis showed coordinated joint-angle patterns across all phases. Walking analysis identified arm swing angles of 50.9°–58.8° and leg separation angles of 64.3°–67.2°, indicating a stable gait rhythm. The running analysis revealed knee angles of 68.8°–69.8° and elbow angles of 87.6°–89.1°, indicating efficient propulsive mechanics. The flight phase demonstrated knee angles of 81.2°–87.8° and elbow angles of 80.4°–88.3°, suggesting effective momentum use and postural stability. These measurements supported stride-efficiency assessment and technique evaluation. Qualitative findings revealed that Kinovea enabled athletes to interpret movement phases and identify technical inefficiencies through slow-motion and frame-by-frame visualization.
Conclusion: Kinovea supports basic motion analysis by providing clear kinematic information and helping beginner athletes observe and refine their movement techniques. The findings also offer practical value for coaches by enabling more precise identification of inefficient patterns and guiding targeted corrections during early-stage training.</jats:p>

title: A Review of Phishing Detection Techniques Using Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing
abstract: <jats:p>The goal of phishing attacks, which rank high among cyber risks, is to steal sensitive information (such as login passwords, financial data, and more) from unsuspecting people and companies. Blacklist, whitelist, rule, heuristic, and signature-based detection methods are no longer suitable due to the rising sophistication of phishing schemes. As a result, ML, DL, and NLP are rapidly becoming into effective instruments for detecting both well-known and brand-new forms of phishing. Background on phishing assaults, old ways of detecting them, and recent advances in intelligent phishing detection are all included in this article. It delves into several machine learning algorithms such as decision tree, LSTM, ANN, CNN, and RNN, as well as deep learning models like KNN, NB, and SVM. Also, natural language processing methods including word embedding, sentiment analysis, text categorization, and tokenization are explored with the aim of detecting phishing material. Presenting a comprehensive, precise, and up-to-the-minute phishing detection system is the ultimate goal of this study, which focuses on machine learning frameworks, performance indicators, present obstacles, and future research directions.</jats:p>

title: HYBRID NETWORK INTRUSION DETECTION SYSTEM BASED ON SIGNATURE ANALYSIS AND MACHINE LEARNING METHODS
abstract: <jats:p>In the context of increasing complexity of modern network infrastructures and the growing number of cyberattacks, improving the effectiveness of intrusion detection systems is a highly relevant task. The aim of this work is to develop and investigate a hybrid approach to network attack detection based on a combination of signature-based analysis and intelligent machine learning methods.  The research methods include analysis of requirements for anomaly detection systems, comparative analysis of existing solutions, design of a hybrid system architecture, and experimental modeling using multiclass classification of network traffic. The results demonstrate that integrating a neural model with a traditional detection system improves attack detection coverage and reduces the number of false positives.  The practical significance of the study lies in the possibility of deploying the proposed architecture in real corporate networks, while the theoretical significance consists in substantiating the effectiveness of a hybrid approach to traffic analysis. Future research directions include adaptive model training and expansion of the range of detectable attacks.</jats:p>

title: Large Language Models in Clinical Neurology: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being evaluated for clinical neurology applications, yet their real-world utility, safety, and deployment readiness remain unclear. This review maps the literature on LLMs applied to text-based and text-derived neurology tasks, characterizing current use cases, evaluation strategies, performance metrics, and reported safety concerns. We identify areas with relatively robust evidence, highlight important evidence gaps, and outline key methodological and clinical barriers that must be addressed before responsible clinical adoption. Following  Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), we searched 4 databases (January 2022 to February 2026) and included 32 studies (2023-2026) spanning 7 neurology subspecialties; 9 were simulation or feasibility studies, 17 analyzed retrospective clinical data, and 6 reported prospective evaluation. Proprietary models predominated; 5 studies used retrieval-augmented generation and 1 used a multiagent framework. Performance was highest for constrained tasks, including binary diagnostic classification (area under the curve 0.75-0.94), information extraction (F1 0.89-0.90), patient-education question answering (accuracy 68%-97%), and ischemic stroke thrombectomy decision support (area under the curve [AUC] 0.92) and lowest for open-ended case-based reasoning (accuracy 42%-54%). Recurrent safety signals included hallucinated and fabricated citations, poor calibration with overconfidence (for example, 100% sensitivity with 27% specificity for epilepsy diagnosis), and a systematic bias toward intervention. On adapted Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies Using Artificial Intelligence (QUADAS-AI) charting, overall risk of bias was low in 1 study (3%), moderate in 16 (50%), and high in 15 (47%), driven chiefly by absent external validation (31/32, 97%). Benchmarked against high-reliability and 6 Sigma standards, reported error rates remain orders of magnitude too high for autonomous use. Evidence for LLMs in neurology is early, heterogeneous, and limited by scarce external and prospective validation. Current data support only narrow, clinician-supervised uses such as documentation and education, while cautioning against autonomous diagnostic or therapeutic use. Rigorous, prospective, externally validated studies with standardized reporting and explicit safety and ethical evaluation are needed before broader adoption. PROSPERO CRD420251082465.

title: Image-Based AI for the Diagnosis of Retinopathy of Prematurity: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is one of the major causes of preventable blindness in premature infants. Early screening, accurate diagnosis, and severity classification are crucial for reducing irreversible visual impairment. Recently, image-based AI models have been widely applied to ROP screening, diagnosis, and severity classification. However, the model architecture, data source, validation method, and diagnostic task vary across studies. Consequently, the overall diagnostic efficiency and clinical utility of deep learning (DL) remain to be systematically assessed. This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of image-based AI for ROP by disease type, validation method, model type, and use of transfer learning (TL). We performed a systematic search across Web of Science, Embase, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, and Cochrane Library as of October 12, 2026, to identify studies investigating image-based AI for ROP detection or clinical subtype classification. The risk of bias (RoB) of included studies was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled using bivariate mixed-effects models, with analyses stratified by diagnostic task and validation method. Sixty-two studies contributed 185 contingency tables. For normal vs ROP, pooled sensitivity was 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.96) and specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.94-0.97). For normal vs treatment-requiring ROP (TR-ROP), sensitivity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.91-0.99) and specificity was 0.74 (95% CI 0.66-0.80). For mild vs severe ROP, specificity was 0.78 (95% CI 0.59-0.90). In external validation, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.95 (95% CI 0.89-0.97) and 0.83 (95% CI 0.72-0.90), respectively, while the corresponding estimates were 0.95 (95% CI 0.93-0.96) and 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) in internal validation. For DL and conventional machine learning (ML) models, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98), respectively, while specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.95-0.97) and 0.91 (95% CI 0.84-0.94), respectively. With and without TL, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.95 (95% CI 0.92-0.97), respectively, while specificity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) and 0.92 (95% CI 0.86-0.95), respectively. Image-based AI may have high sensitivity for ROP assessment, but its specificity is lower for identifying TR-ROP and in the external-validation subgroup. Given the predominance of retrospective studies, heterogeneity, and limited external validation, current evidence supports AI as an adjunct to screening and referral, with clinicians retaining responsibility for diagnostic and treatment decisions. Prospective, multicenter external validation is needed. PROSPERO CRD420261418502; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261418502.

title: Comprehensive Clinical Decision-Support Framework for Obesity Prevention Using Large-Scale Health Checkup Data: Development and Evaluation Study.
abstract: Obesity prevention requires identifying nonobese adults at risk of developing obesity. Routine health checkups collect anthropometric, laboratory, medical history, and lifestyle information, but screening primarily describes current anthropometric status and does not directly provide individualized estimates of future risk for preventive counseling. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a comprehensive clinical decision-support framework for obesity prevention using large-scale health checkup data. This retrospective cohort study used repeated examination data from the Kangbuk Samsung Health Study. Adults with BMI less than 25 kg/m², at least 3 health checkup visits, a 2-year obesity-free washout period, and postindex follow-up were included. Incident obesity was defined as the first follow-up BMI of 25 kg/m² or higher. The framework integrated a single-visit prediction tier (which we termed lite), a survival component for time-to-transition context, a repeated-measurement updating tier (which we termed plus), and an explainability layer. The primary lite-tier and survival analyses used training-set-only imputation. A previously exported lite-tier Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) component was externally evaluated in 328,268 National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) participants. Among 231,683 initially nonobese participants, 38,094 developed incident obesity. In the aligned 5-year visit-1 test cohort, 4088 of 21,783 (18.8%) participants developed obesity. The lite-tier ensemble achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918, an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.693, a Brier score of 0.087, and an expected calibration error of 0.005. AUPRC was approximately 3.7 times the no-information reference. AUROCs were 0.913 for BMI-only and 0.914 for BMI+age+sex. Observed 5-year incidence ranged from 0.1% (6/4357) to 64.7% (2821/4357) across accelerated failure time (AFT) risk quintiles. The plus tier achieved a landmark-row AUROC of 0.899 with less favorable calibration. The previously exported lite-tier XGBoost component achieved an external AUROC of 0.857, AUPRC of 0.575, and Brier score of 0.132. Large-scale health checkup data supported an integrated framework for single-visit triage, temporal risk context, risk-domain explanation, and exploratory repeated-measurement updating, providing a basis for prevention-oriented risk communication and follow-up prioritization. The overall gain in discrimination beyond BMI was modest, and the effects on clinical decisions and obesity prevention require prospective evaluation.

title: Factors Influencing Older Adults' Sustained Engagement in Digital Psychological Interventions in Resource-Limited Settings: Qualitative Study Guided by the Social Ecological Model.
abstract: Digital behavioral activation therapy (DBAT) is effective in reducing late-life depression (LLD). However, older adults in resource-limited settings often show low adherence and retention. This pattern is largely driven by the digital divide. Digital inclusion offers a pathway to address this gap by recognizing older adults as active participants rather than passive recipients. Despite this potential, limited research has examined low engagement from the perspective of older adults' lived experiences. This gap restricts understanding of the complex factors that shape engagement in digital psychological interventions. This study aimed to systematically explore, through the lens of digital inclusion and guided by the social ecological model, the multilevel factors influencing older adults' sustained engagement in digital psychological interventions within resource-limited settings, specifically focusing on the lived experiences of retained users who completed the full program. A descriptive phenomenological design was used. Semistructured interviews were conducted with older adults in Western Hunan, China. Data were transcribed using machine-assisted methods and verified manually. Data were analyzed using the Colaizzi phenomenological method combined with thematic and framework analysis guided by the social ecological model. Two researchers independently coded the data and refined themes through discussion. Nineteen older adults with LLD from resource-limited settings were included. Engagement in DBAT was shaped by factors across multiple levels. At the individual level, factors included health needs, learning motivation, physiological and cognitive limitations, and low digital literacy. At the interpersonal level, factors included intergenerational support, emotional burden, established social networks, and digital exclusion. At the society level, available devices and networks sometimes hindered engagement due to poor age-friendly design and unstable connectivity. Personal aspirations for digital participation often conflicted with social resistance. At the policy level, financial burden, standardized policy approaches, and unmet individual needs limited engagement. These factors interacted to influence engagement behavior. This study identifies multilevel factors shaping older adults' sustained engagement in digital psychological interventions within resource-limited settings, reflecting the experiences of retained users. The findings advocate for integrated, context-sensitive strategies grounded in a digital inclusion framework. Crucially, nurses play a key role in promoting technology access, improving digital literacy, supporting social participation, and advocating for equitable services. These efforts can enhance accessibility and adherence, ultimately fostering more equitable and sustainable digital mental health care for vulnerable aging populations. title: Measure the Ward First: Intentional Sufficiency as a Design Rule for Sleep Sensing in Acute Inpatient Psychiatry.
abstract: This Viewpoint argues that measurement design, not model capability, is the first constraint on clinical AI in acute inpatient psychiatry and proposes intentional sufficiency as a design rule for sleep sensing on acute wards. Acute psychiatric wards exclude much of the conventional sensing design space: ligature, ingestion, and projectile hazards; unreliable adherence; impaired consent; and nursing workload mean that a device that is excellent when a patient is cooperative may be absent when the patient is most unwell. We define intentional sufficiency in 3 parts: the intended clinical use sets the required signal properties and acceptable error; safety, validity, consent, and workflow constraints define the feasible design space; and within that space, the rule selects the least burdensome option that preserves the required properties, because excess capability can be paid for in persistence, not only in money. We contrast this rule with capability-maximizing design using 2 examples at opposite ends of the design space: a structured nightly nursing sleep duration record that, in Taiwan, already exists within routine care, and a disposable wrist-worn sensing architecture under development that reduces the wearable to what the derived sleep measure requires. The first shows when the rule can conclude that no hardware should be added, provided adequacy has been shown for the intended use; the second shows when it concludes that hardware must be redesigned, and is presented as a design prediction rather than a result. Importantly, agreement with a reference method does not by itself establish task-level sufficiency; greater sensing capability does not necessarily produce more clinically available information when deployment and persistence are constrained; and some signal properties are validity defining and cannot be traded against cost.

title: A mHealth-Based Vestibular Rehabilitation Program for Postoperative Vestibular Dysfunction in Patients With Vestibular Schwannoma: Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Patients with vestibular schwannoma often experience postoperative vestibular dysfunction, including vertigo, dizziness, and imbalance, which severely impair daily functioning and quality of life. Effective and accessible rehabilitation strategies are needed to improve recovery after surgery. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a mobile health-based vestibular rehabilitation program in improving postoperative vestibular outcomes after unilateral vestibular schwannoma surgery. A prospective randomized controlled trial comparing a customized mobile app-based vestibular rehabilitation program with standard face-to-face vestibular rehabilitation was conducted at the Otology Center, Eye & ENT Hospital, Fudan University, from October 2023 to May 2025. A total of 60 patients undergoing unilateral vestibular schwannoma surgery were enrolled and randomly assigned to either an intervention group (n=30) or a control group (n=30). Both groups received a 90-day vestibular rehabilitation program. The intervention group received guidance, symptom recording, and adherence monitoring through a customized mobile app, whereas the control group received face-to-face guidance. The primary outcome was the between-group difference in the change in Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI) score from baseline (preoperative) to postoperative day 90. Secondary outcomes included visual analog scale scores for vestibular symptoms and the incidence of vertigo, dizziness, vestibulo-visual symptoms, and postural symptoms. Of the 60 randomized participants, 52 (86.7%) had DHI scores available at postoperative day 90, and 49 (81.7%) had paired baseline and day-90 DHI scores available to calculate the primary outcome. The adjusted between-group difference in DHI change from baseline to postoperative day 90 was not significant (adjusted mean difference -0.83, 95% CI -8.79 to 7.13; P=.84). No significant differences were observed in visual analog scale scores at postoperative days 7, 30, or 90 (all P>.05). Among the assessed vestibular symptoms, postural symptoms on postoperative day 7 were reported by 53.3% (16/30) of the intervention group and 83.3% (25/30) of the control group; the difference was not significant after Holm adjustment (unadjusted P=.03; Holm-adjusted P=.30). In conclusion, mobile health-based rehabilitation did not demonstrate greater improvement in postoperative vestibular outcomes than face-to-face rehabilitation following unilateral vestibular schwannoma surgery. The lower proportion of patients reporting postural symptoms on postoperative day 7 remains an exploratory finding requiring confirmation in future studies. title: A "Basin of Attraction" Theory of Speech Initiation and Stuttering.
abstract: Recent work in motor neuroscience suggests that well-learned actions are implemented as stable, stereotyped trajectories in neural state space. The purpose of this article was to propose a theory of the neural basis of speech initiation that extends this idea to speech production and identifies a specific disruption that may underlie speech dysfluencies in stuttering. We advance a conceptual framework in which the motor program for a familiar word corresponds to a stable neural trajectory with an associated basin of attraction. We integrate findings from primate motor control, human speech neuroscience, and basal ganglia physiology to specify the role of the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical (BGTC) circuit in initiating these trajectories. We propose that fluent speech depends on the ability of the BGTC circuit to steer the distributed speech motor network into the basin of attraction of the upcoming word's motor program. Stuttering arises when this process is unreliable or poorly coordinated, preventing the motor program from being executed until the neural state is corrected or the effective basin of attraction is broadened through compensatory mechanisms. The basin of attraction framework provides a mechanistic description of the proximal neural processes responsible for stuttering events that can account for a wide range of behavioral and neurophysiological findings in stuttering. It also aligns stuttering theory with contemporary dynamical systems approaches to motor control and generates testable predictions for future neurophysiological and neuroimaging studies.

title: Caregiver-Informed Safety and System Requirements for Real-Time Feedback During Pediatric Inhaler Use: Qualitative Concept-Elicitation Study.
abstract: Correct use of a pressurized metered-dose inhaler (pMDI), usually with a valved holding chamber, depends on use-related conditions that caregivers may not observe directly, including inhalation pattern, actuation-inhalation timing, mask seal, and device orientation. Many digital inhaler systems emphasize actuation or adherence. Systems that infer technique-related conditions from proxy signals may add real-time feedback but also create false reassurance if a positive state is displayed when evidence is inadequate. Caregiver expectations for such feedback and its failure states remain poorly characterized before prototype development. This study aimed to characterize caregivers' experiences of pediatric inhaler administration and translate responses to a proposed sensor concept into traceable candidate safety, system, and validation requirements. We conducted 23 semistructured concept-elicitation sessions through Zoom videoconference with 27 caregivers of children who currently or previously used a pMDI. Interviews consisted of 19 individual and 4 dyadic sessions pairing 2 caregivers from different households. Sessions were conducted remotely between April and July 2026 from the University of Calgary, Alberta, Canada. Recruitment originated in Calgary and was not geographically restricted. A 6-phase guide examined current practices, difficulties, prior digital-tool use, and responses to a screen-shared clip-on concept incorporating airflow-, timing-, seal-, and orientation-related sensing; on-device feedback; an optional child-facing app; and a caregiver dashboard. No working prototype was evaluated. Approximately 86,000 transcript words underwent hybrid directed and conventional qualitative content analysis using an 18-category codebook. Two researchers independently coded the complete 27×18 matrix (486 paired decisions) across 2 rounds. Consensus categories were translated into candidate requirements and assigned an earliest verification or evaluation locus. Counts are descriptive caregiver-voice tallies, not prevalence estimates. Persistent uncertainty about whether administration conditions were adequate was the dominant lived experience (19/27); for 5 caregivers, existing passive cues had not resolved it. A simple, real-time on-device signal was endorsed by 25 caregivers, but willingness to consider the concept was conditional on reliability (9 caregivers named reasons for abandonment, notably a "false green"), low-friction operation during acute symptoms (12/27), minimal added bulk and technique change, and one or more of clinical validation, clinician recommendation, or a trial pathway (composite category; 23/27). Stances on gamification (20/27), dashboard cadence (18/27), aesthetics (24/27), and privacy (18/27) supported an optional, configurable software layer. Intercoder agreement was 94% (Cohen κ=0.88). The analytic synthesis yielded a conceptual architecture separating observable proxy signals, an inference and data-quality gate, and positive, corrective, or uncertain feedback states. Participating caregivers prioritized immediate and interpretable feedback about use-related conditions. The findings support conservative state assignment, an explicit uncertain state for indeterminate signals, and app-independent acute-use feedback. These are candidate requirements rather than validated device specifications; subsequent work should proceed through bench verification, simulated-use human factors evaluation, and prospective clinical or field validation.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Radiomics-Based Machine Learning in Differentiating Glioblastoma From Brain Metastasis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) and brain metastasis (BM) are the most common malignant intracranial tumors in adults. Noninvasive differentiation between them remains challenging, as they frequently share similar imaging features. Although radiomics-based machine learning (ML) models show promise, systematic evidence of their performance remains limited. We aimed to systematically estimate the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based ML models in differentiating GBM from BM and to explore multiclass classification involving primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL), thereby assessing their potential for clinical use. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases from inception to January 22, 2026, for studies reporting the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based ML models for differentiating GBM from BM. Multiclass studies involving PCNSL were also retained. Methodological quality was appraised via the Radiomics Quality Score 2.0. Binary diagnostic accuracy was pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, stratified by internal and independent external validation. Multiclass sensitivities and specificities were pooled using separate joint generalized linear mixed models. Physician assessments were evaluated as an exploratory benchmark. A total of 39 studies (31 binary and 8 multiclass), involving 11,558 patients, were included. For binary classification, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 88.9% (95% CI 84.1%-92.4%) and 83.0% (95% CI 76.8%-87.9%) in internal validation, and 83.8% (95% CI 77.4%-88.7%) and 80.7% (95% CI 71.1%-87.7%) in external validation, respectively. In multiclass analyses, pooled sensitivity was 84.4% (95% CI 72.4%-91.8%) for GBM, 70.6% (95% CI 54.4%-82.8%) for BM, and 75.0% (95% CI 62.7%-84.3%) for PCNSL, with corresponding specificities of 82.5% (95% CI 70.1%-90.4%), 88.8% (95% CI 81.9%-93.3%), and 94.4% (95% CI 88.4%-97.4%), respectively. Radiomics-based ML models could distinguish between GBM and BM in the included cohorts. However, due to methodological limitations and scarce evidence, their generalizability and clinical utility remain unclear. Further multicenter prospective studies should conduct independent external validation in consecutive patients. PROSPERO CRD420261295269; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261295269.

title: Pharmacometrics, Artificial Intelligence, and Machine Learning in Precision Dosing and Clinical Toxicology.
abstract: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) enables individualized pharmacotherapy for drugs with high interpatient variability and concentration-dependent effects. Conventional Bayesian approaches, although clinically established, may not fully capture pharmacokinetic complexity in dynamic or heterogeneous patient populations. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning methods offer complementary capabilities, including modeling nonlinear relationships and integrating high-dimensional clinical data. Peer-reviewed studies that applied AI or machine-learning methods to TDM between January 2017 and April 2026 were reviewed in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines. Studies involving adult and pediatric populations were included, whereas reviews, editorials, and animal studies were excluded. Forty-seven studies covering a range of drugs, including vancomycin, tacrolimus, antiepileptics, mycophenolic acid, methotrexate, and voriconazole, were included. Tree-based ensemble methods, particularly eXtreme Gradient Boosting, random forest, and gradient boosting, were the most frequently applied algorithms. In general, these methods demonstrated strong predictive performance, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values up to 0.90 for classification tasks and coefficient of determination values up to 0.85 for regression tasks. In 13 studies, AI models demonstrated predictive performance comparable with or exceeding that of traditional population pharmacokinetic and Bayesian approaches for selected applications. However, these comparisons were heterogeneous and often based on retrospective data sets with limited external validation. AI-based methods have considerable potential for enhancing TDM, particularly for dose optimization, drug-exposure estimation, and toxicity prediction. However, evidence linking improved predictive performance to meaningful clinical outcomes remains limited.
ai_summary: AI and machine-learning methods offer complementary capabilities, including modeling nonlinear relationships and integrating high-dimensional clinical data . Peer-reviewed studies that applied AI or machine- learning methods to TDM between January 2017 and April 2026 were reviewed .

title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
abstract: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.
ai_summary: Theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure . calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own .

title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
abstract: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. We propose Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), which uses binary safety labels to construct harmful and benign prototypes and makes predictions from relative prototype distances. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation. In our setup, it uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier. Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI's detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points. Using the same encoder, JDPI achieves slightly higher ROC-AUC on one benchmark and stays within 0.017 of the baseline across all four. With dataset-specific adaptation, JDPI exceeds the released Llama Guard 3-8B baseline by 0.173-0.310 in ROC-AUC across the four benchmarks. In multi-turn replay on TomGibbs, JDPI uses accumulated user history as the conversation unfolds, achieving higher conversation-level accuracy than when it uses the current turn alone. Across 12 directed transfers, JDPI outperforms the classifier by an average of 1.59 percentage points in accuracy, demonstrating stronger cross-dataset robustness.
ai_summary: JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation . It uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier . Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPi's detection accuracy by 9.

title: Mapping the AI Supply Chain: Dependencies, Vulnerabilities, and Market Concentration in the AI Ecosystem
abstract: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets. While the layers of the AI stack are relatively well understood, the relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented. In this work, we focus on the organizations that make up the AI supply chain: the complex network of actors that contribute to the development and deployment of AI. We motivate the examination of the organizational AI supply chain---highlighting concerns about concentration, power, chokepoints, cascading failures, fragmented accountability, and risk---then describe our pipeline for mapping the AI supply chain. Our pipeline yields our main contribution: a multilayered, large-scale dataset of actors and relationships in the AI ecosystem, annotated with dates, descriptions, types, tags, and more. This work takes a step toward systematically mapping and measuring the AI supply chain and its properties, cataloging how models, data, chips, infrastructure, capital, and even talent flow between organizations. This data enable critical examinations of industry relationships and yield insights into the political economy of AI development and concentration. We provide several illustrative analyses, including studying the most central actors, analyzing network concentration, and identifying communities and chokepoints. While our dataset is fairly comprehensive, it is also necessarily incomplete: public documents omit private deals, and coverage is shaped by search design. Together, the approach, data, and findings aim to serve as a resource for studying the AI ecosystem. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarahcen/ai-supply-chain and can be explored interactively at https://aisupplychains.org/.
ai_summary: AI systems are built across many organizations that contribute models, data, compute, capital, talent, and other assets . The relationships between actors and components across layers remains sparsely documented .

title: $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling
abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.
ai_summary: $Z$-sight is a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling . The model is based on video-based world action models (WAMs)

title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
abstract: Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. However, existing harness evolution methods often overlook implicit requirements and interaction needs, while using a single evolution agent to modify the harness and benchmark scores to select changes. This process often produces narrow patches and leads to benchmark-specific local optima. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered loop that brings real-world engineering practices into harness evolution. The loop consists of three steps: (1) User-driven evaluation lets simulated users raise their requirements as issues while they work with the harness over multiple turns. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. (3) Requirement-driven selection merges a change only when it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. Empirically, on held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% while using 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, and achieves higher pass@1 than Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE. In a blind human A/B test, real users prefer AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid pairs and rate it higher on all five dimensions, matching the directional preference of the user simulator. The human A/B results show that AHE-Beta achieves its goal of aligning harness evolution with real-world user requirements. Without further evolution, the gains transfer to GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with pass@1 improvements of 15.8% and 5.3% over Base Harness. Together, these results show that requirement-centered harness evolution is a more general method for improving agent capabilities.

title: UltraTex: Aligning Physical Knowledge for High-Fidelity PBR Texture Generation
abstract: Generating physically based rendering (PBR) texture maps for a 3D mesh from a single reference image is highly ambiguous, as the observed appearance entangles material identity, surface reflectance, and illumination. While current generative methods produce realistic albedo maps, they still struggle to infer accurate metallic and roughness attributes for relighting. We present UltraTex, a cascaded multi-view framework that moves beyond appearance matching by integrating physical knowledge into multi-view diffusion-based PBR generation. UltraTex first jointly predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to generate more detailed albedo maps, and then predicts metallic-roughness (MR) maps conditioned on the generated albedo, reference image, and material semantic priors. To inject material semantics, a lightweight adapter transforms hidden-layer features of a vision-language model (VLM) into intrinsic material representation tokens, providing part-level knowledge anchors for MR estimation. To model material-light interaction, photometric representation alignment guides intermediate diffusion features toward ground-truth material renderings under controlled lighting. This makes metallic and roughness variations observable through highlight intensity, specular sharpness, and local reflectance contrast, providing stronger guidance for fine-grained material prediction without explicit lighting supervision. Extensive experiments show that UltraTex generates high-quality textures and outperforms existing open-source and commercial methods in visual fidelity, material accuracy, and physical plausibility.
ai_summary: UltraTex is a cascaded multi-view framework that moves beyond appearance matching by integrating physical knowledge into multi- view diffusion-based PBR generation . UltraTex first predicts albedo and world-space shading normals to generate more detailed albeda maps .

title: Unified Law for Visual Tasks (The Four Laws of Computer Vision)
abstract: In this paper, we propose a Unified Law for Visual Tasks, which could be further divided into Four Laws of Computer Vision, with the goal of enabling a single framework or method to uniformly train on and perform nearly all visual tasks. Our starting point is an inspiration and hypothesis: if the world information is encoded into image, which we call World Snapshots, then image processing is world processing, and image generation is World Snapshot generation. Furthermore, if all visual and visualization tasks can be reformulated as generation tasks, then a unified method, World Snapshot Models (WSMs), can perform the vast majority of visual tasks, much as large language models have largely unified natural language processing. This paper validates these laws across more than 1,000 trained and evaluated visual tasks (defined by distinct input-output mappings) and presents a unified training framework for future visual-task research and applications.
ai_summary: A Unified Law for Visual Tasks could be further divided into Four Laws of Computer Vision . The paper validates these laws across more than 1,000 trained and evaluated visual tasks . It presents a unified training framework for future visual-task research and applications .

title: PrismRestore: A Compact Restoration Toolbox for Agentic Image Restoration
abstract: Agentic image restoration composes operations to handle mixed degradations, yet its toolbox often requires storing multiple restoration networks. We propose PrismRestore, which constructs a compact bank of callable restoration actions from a single frozen all-in-one model. Our approach builds on task-dependent yet overlapping channel responses in the shared model. An offline task-prior search uses activation and gradient statistics to group channels with similar response profiles, then searches task-specific modulation coefficients over non-representative channels while leaving representative channels unmodulated. The resulting prior bank enables explicit action selection and composition without additional restoration backbones or task-specific adapter modules. A state-conditioned policy learns to compose these actions using Group Relative Policy Optimization. Its objective separately normalizes fidelity and perceptual feedback within groups of trajectories sampled for the same input, and combines terminal evaluation with return-to-go derived from stepwise quality changes. Experiments on synthetic composite-degradation and real-world multi-task benchmarks show improvements over the evaluated all-in-one baselines and restoration quality competitive with multi-model agents. PrismRestore achieves these results with a single restoration backbone and faster inference than the evaluated agentic baselines.
ai_summary: PrismRestore constructs a compact bank of callable restoration actions from a single frozen all-in-one model . An offline task-prior search uses activation and gradient statistics to group channels with similar response profiles .

title: Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation
abstract: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.
ai_summary: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model . We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement .

title: ShadowTransfer: A Geographic Transfer Benchmark for Overhead Shadow Detection
abstract: Overhead aerial imagery feeds dense-prediction pipelines that are routinely trained in one geographic region and deployed in another, yet no benchmark measures how shadow detection models transfer across regions. Existing overhead shadow datasets either lack a geographic transfer protocol or rely on automatically generated labels. We introduce ShadowTransfer, a benchmark of 4,500 human-verified shadow masks across three U.S. cities at two native resolutions, paired with a leave-one-city-out evaluation protocol. Under vanilla training, holding out the test city costs 3.5 to 7.8 mIoU across four architectures, the gap remains significant when the training set grows from 225 to 900 images, and six of eight adaptation methods degrade more than vanilla training on average. We propose a three-probe framework that diagnoses where and how the transfer breaks: the failure operates in feature space, beyond the reach of pixel-histogram matching, shows up as a confidence collapse on shadow pixels while background confidence stays intact, and is recoverable by retraining different architectural components depending on the model: encoder for some, decoder for others. These findings replicate on INRIA building footprints, suggesting they describe geographic transfer beyond shadows. Guided by the diagnosis, we build Spectral Information Bottleneck (SIB), a plug-in module with one component per finding. Across the 9 (architecture, held-out city) cells, SIB has the smallest mean gap to the within-city upper bound of the ten methods we evaluate (6.42 mIoU), level with FDA. The benchmark, LOCO protocol, code, and trained models are released to support reproducible evaluation of geographic transfer in overhead dense prediction.
ai_summary: ShadowTransfer is a benchmark of 4,500 human-verified shadow masks across three U.S. cities . The benchmark is paired with a leave-one-city-out evaluation protocol . Under vanilla training, holding out the test city costs 3.5 to 7.8 mIoU across four architectures .

title: Mine Locally, Verify Globally: Exact Recovery, Compilation, and Distortion of Mined Temporal Rules
abstract: Specification mining extracts temporal rules that describe relationships between events in recorded system traces. Applying these rules in distributed monitoring systems is more difficult because observations come from different nodes, whose clocks may not be synchronized, and events may be lost or reordered during transmission. In this paper, we study how to aggregate the coverage of mined rules across observers, determine whether their temporal windows are needed during monitoring, and characterize their detection under event loss. Our evaluation uses IPv6 packet traces collected from 21 receivers across four continents. We show that local mining followed by global confirmation recovers centralized rule coverage under suitable conditions while substantially reducing communication overhead. In contrast, merging traces with unaligned clocks can distort coverage by introducing incorrect temporal matches. A window-gain criterion identifies rules that require temporal state, while our loss analysis and broker experiments demonstrate why contiguous losses can be more damaging than independent losses. The results identify separate requirements for aggregating observations, selecting monitor state, and handling event loss.
ai_summary: Specification mining extracts temporal rules that describe relationships between events in recorded system traces . Applying these rules in distributed monitoring systems is more difficult because observations come from different nodes . In contrast, merging traces with unaligned clocks can distort coverage by introducing incorrect temporal matches .

title: "I Don't Think It's a Scam": A First Look at Family Intervention Barriers in Elder Abuse Discussions on Reddit and Baidu Tieba
abstract: When older adults trust scammers despite warnings, families face obstacles to intervention. Complainants aged 60 and older reported \$4.9 billion in losses in 2024 to the U.S. Internet Crime Complaint Center. To investigate family intervention barriers to elder scams, we collected 2M Reddit posts from May 2021 to June 2026 and 2B Baidu Tieba posts from 2007 to 2026. The final corpora contain 13,082 Reddit posts and 3,933 Baidu Tieba posts, labeled using platform-specific codebooks, manual reference annotations, and LLM coding. Through a mixed-methods analysis, we find that scams often extend beyond a single incident and are reported alongside debt problems and broken family relationships. In 68.0\% of Reddit posts recording reactions, older adults showed resistance or continued involvement; in Baidu Tieba family-confrontation posts, 41.9\% showed continued belief. Relatives identified fraud in 74.4\% of Reddit posts and narrated cases on Baidu Tieba, but without the victim's consent, relatives may lack the legal authority to intervene. In Reddit posts recording reactions, account locks or credential changes appeared in 8.9\% under resistance or continued involvement, compared with 33.3\% under acceptance. Measures such as phone or network monitoring and financial takeover were reported more often under resistance. Recovering funds is very limited in posts recording follow-up results of fraud; Baidu Tieba users reported that police classified older adults' voluntary transfers as civil disputes.
ai_summary: Complainants aged 60 and older reported $4.9 billion in losses in 2024 to the U.S. Internet Crime Complaint Center . We found that scams often extend beyond a single incident .

title: Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators
abstract: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures.
ai_summary: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations . We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data .

title: ProvCards: Artifact-Oriented Provenance for Heterogeneous Scientific Workflows
abstract: Reproducibility in scientific workflows is hindered by heterogeneous components and execution environments, as well as fragmented provenance capture. Although existing approaches offer established semantics and workflow-specific solutions, provenance remains difficult to capture, exchange, and compose across workflow boundaries. We present ProvCards, an artifact-oriented approach that treats provenance as a first-class artifact grounded in the W3C PROV Data Model. Individual workflow components can generate cards that are stored, exchanged, reused, and composed independently of any workflow system or centralized execution context. ProvDecks group related cards into portable scopes while preserving their identities. ProvGraphs provide derived views for provenance reconstruction, querying, visualization, and analysis. Together, these representations support coherent, task-specific provenance views across heterogeneous components, facilitating traceability, reuse, and reproducibility. We implement ProvCards using a graph-based infrastructure and evaluate them in a scientific data-processing workflow. The results demonstrate independent provenance capture at the component level, composition across component boundaries, and reconstruction for querying and analysis. ProvCards provide a portable, composable, and incrementally extensible foundation for provenance management in heterogeneous scientific workflows.
ai_summary: ProvCards is an artifact-oriented approach that treats provenance as a first-class artifact grounded in the W3C PROV Data Model . ProvDecks group related cards into portable scopes while preserving their identities . ProvGraphs provide derived views for provenance reconstruction, querying, visualization, and analysis .

title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
abstract: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.
ai_summary: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents . But how to assess their quality remains underexplored . It is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior .

title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.
ai_summary: Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding . It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune . It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its fixed-rate precursor .

title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.
ai_summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game . They propose a harder challenge to replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human . They use a dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication .

title: Ground, Iterate, Trace: Decomposing AI Research Ideation
abstract: Large language models have been widely used to generate plausible research ideas, yet it remains unclear what makes automated ideation effective and how generated novel proposals arise from prior scientific work. We introduce the Creative AI Researcher (CAR), an agentic framework combining literature grounding, iterative development and explicit conceptual operators. CAR constructs a semantic knowledge graph from retrieved literature and equips an ideation agent with graph-retrieval tools and four operators: bisociation, analogy, exploration and elaboration. Each operator call is checked against structural acceptance conditions and recorded, producing a trace of intermediate transformations and declared literature sources. We evaluate CAR with two language-model backbones across 40 LiveIdeaBench research topics and two execution benchmarks. CAR achieves significantly higher methodological novelty (MN) than single-shot prompting and The AI Scientist. Its methodological novelty does not differ significantly from the Research Ideation Agent, while its feasibility scores are higher on both backbones. With a shared experiment executor, CAR achieves the highest pairwise win rate among the evaluated AI methods on FML-bench-Lite and BioXArena. In a ten-condition ablation study, MN point estimates favor CAR over one-step proposal on both backbones, but no MN contrast survives correction for multiple comparisons. The results do not establish a consistent quality benefit from explicit operators beyond free-form iteration. CAR makes the sequence of operations and declared literature sources inspectable, separating judged idea quality from procedural traceability.
ai_summary: Large language models have been widely used to generate plausible research ideas . It remains unclear what makes automated ideation effective and how generated novel proposals arise from prior scientific work .

title: Monoculture Robust Learning
abstract: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is $ρ$-replicable, then running it independently $k$ times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with $k$, controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and $ρ$. We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to $γ$ can require a sample-size multiplier of $t = Ω(\log(1/γ))$.
ai_summary: We ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses . We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error .

title: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.
ai_summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics . It drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand . In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment .

title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.
ai_summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models . They promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it . We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked .

title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation
abstract: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.
ai_summary: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation . But controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge . We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate.

title: TangentPDE: Learning Local Operator Responses with Sparse Finite-Difference Supervision
abstract: Neural PDE operators are often optimized through state reconstruction, which largely constrains operator values at observed inputs but does not fully characterize their sensitivity to local perturbations. A more faithful approximation of operator behavior requires not only accurate state predictions, but also correct variations along local perturbation directions. We present TangentPDE, which uses finite differences to approximate directional derivatives and constructs task-relevant finite-step responses from the state outputs of a reference solver at sparse paired inputs. Its objective jointly constrains state fidelity, response-direction alignment, and response-magnitude calibration, thereby learning both operator values and their local variations. Because the response labels are constructed solely from state outputs at paired inputs, the method requires neither explicit derivative labels, linearized or adjoint PDE solves, nor full Jacobians, and remains applicable to nonlinear solvers without derivative interfaces. Building on this, we additionally propose a selectively executed adaptation mechanism to strengthen local operator representations under finite-difference supervision. Budget-matched and correspondence-perturbed controls isolate the effect of relational supervision from improvements attributable to additional state observations or increased data volume. Designed as a plug-and-play training framework, TangentPDE integrates with diverse neural-operator backbones. Across four PDE systems and 20 task-backbone settings, TangentPDE lowers the three-seed mean state error in 18 settings and the corresponding Rollout@20 error in 18, while intrinsic finite-step response gains are strongest on DiffReact and remain task- and backbone-dependent elsewhere.

TangentPDE uses finite differences to approximate directional derivatives and constructs task-relevant finite-step responses from the state outputs of a reference solver at sparse paired inputs .

title: MicroAssert: Microarchitecture-Aware Structured Assertion Generation for CPU Verification
abstract: Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs. We present MicroAssert, a microarchitecture-aware framework that identifies functional regions directly from RTL and generates local and composite assertions through structured contracts and deterministic verification primitives. Coverage-guided feedback further improves verification completeness by progressively expanding proof-relevant RTL coverage. Evaluated on five open-source RISC-V CPUs against three existing assertion generation approaches, MicroAssert achieves 100% syntax correctness and complete branch, statement, and toggle coverage, with an average proven rate of 74.82% and Proof Core coverage of 90.96%. Mutation testing further demonstrates its advantage, achieving an average error detection rate of 28.73%, 1.99 to 3.51 times higher than existing methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of microarchitecture-aware assertion generation.
ai_summary: Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs . We present MicroAssert, a microarch architecture-aware framework that identifies functional regions directly from RTL and generates local and composite assertions .

title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states . The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes .

title: Choosing What to Observe: Budget-Paired Counterfactual Audits for Credible Evaluation of Visual Agents
abstract: Visual agents that read dense documents must ration a finite observation budget across candidate regions, yet answer accuracy conflates where an agent looks, how it adapts to the reads that remain, and how it an?swers once observation stops.
